script.opening: "Sorry to ring — it’s my dodgy knee again, the arthritis one. It’s blown up like a balloon over the last day or so, red hot and I can’t put any weight on it. I had one of those steroid injections in it last week. I just need some stronger painkillers really, and I’ll rest it and wait for it to settle like it usually does. Don’t want to make a fuss over a bad knee."

facts.text: If explored: a SINGLE knee, acutely HOT, SWOLLEN, RED, exquisitely painful, unable to weight-bear or move it — over ~36 hours. This monoarticular, hot, acutely painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — a joint-destroying emergency.

On questioning: a STEROID JOINT INJECTION 10 days ago (direct portal for infection), DIABETES (immunocompromise), age, pre-existing joint disease — all major risk factors for septic arthritis. He frames the injection as reassuring ("it’s been seen to") rather than a risk.

If asked: feeling shivery, rough, possibly feverish; hasn’t checked his temperature; sugars "all over the place". Systemic upset raises sepsis concern. He minimises all of this as "just feeling run down with the pain".

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "don’t want to make a fuss / wait it out" is partly stoicism and partly FEAR of hospital: his wife was recently admitted and died in hospital after a fall, and he is frightened of going in himself ("people don’t come out"). He is downplaying genuinely emergency features to stay home. The grief and fear must be heard, or he won’t go.

Officially: stronger painkillers and to wait it out at home. What he needs: recognition that a hot, swollen, non-weight-bearing single joint (post-injection, diabetic, systemically unwell) is a septic-arthritis emergency requiring same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration — with his hospital fear and grief handled so he agrees to go.

ice.ideas: It’s just a bad flare of his knee arthritis; painkillers and rest will settle it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of hospital after his wife died there following an admission ("people don’t come out"); he’s minimising emergency features to avoid going in, framing the recent injection as reassurance rather than a risk.
ice.expectations: Stronger painkillers to wait it out at home. What he actually needs: urgent same-day hospital assessment for possible septic arthritis (joint aspiration), with his hospital fear and grief addressed.

cues: Single hot, swollen, red, non-weight-bearing joint over ~36h — septic arthritis until proven otherwise; not "just arthritis".
Steroid injection 10 days ago + diabetes + feeling shivery — stacked risk factors and systemic upset.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a SINGLE acutely hot, swollen, red, painful joint with inability to weight-bear as SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise — and does NOT accept the "just an arthritis flare" framing or prescribe painkillers to wait it out

Weights the major risk factors: recent intra-articular STEROID INJECTION (portal of entry), DIABETES (immunocompromise), age and pre-existing joint disease — and recognises the recent injection raises, not lowers, concern

Screens for systemic infection/sepsis (fever, rigors, malaise; by phone the NICE NG253 red flags — new confusion or altered mental state, breathlessness, mottled or ashen skin, not passing urine — any of which means a 999 ambulance; his erratic sugars matter for his diabetes but are not an NG253 sepsis criterion) and recognises that septic arthritis can be present even without florid systemic features; does not require fever to act

Arranges URGENT same-day hospital assessment (acute/orthopaedics/ED) for joint ASPIRATION (before antibiotics where possible — BSR/BHPR 2006: aspirate, Gram-stain and culture synovial fluid before antibiotics, with crystal microscopy) and management — recognising septic arthritis is a joint-destroying emergency that cannot be diagnosed or excluded by phone

Considers the differential without false reassurance (gout/pseudogout, reactive, crystal flare) but knows that septic arthritis MUST be excluded by aspiration first — a crystal/OA history does not exclude infection (they can coexist)
Hears the hospital fear and the grief about his wife, and addresses them with compassion — using them to bring him TO assessment rather than dismissing or overriding him
Conveys urgency clearly without panic, and does not collude with "wait it out"; explains why same-day matters (a joint can be destroyed in days, sepsis risk)

Safety-nets and acts: arranges the same-day pathway and confirms he will go; what to watch (worsening, high fever, confusion → 999); does not give a prescription-and-wait plan; documents and follows up to ensure he was seen

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang, Stan — but I have to be honest, because this matters: a knee that’s suddenly hot, red, swollen and that you can’t weight-bear on, all in a day or so, isn’t a normal arthritis flare. That picture can mean an infection IN the joint, and that’s something we treat as an emergency, not something to wait out."

"And the steroid injection last week — I know it feels like the knee’s ‘been seen to’, but actually that’s one of the things that makes me MORE concerned, because any injection into a joint can occasionally let infection in. With your diabetes on top, your body’s less able to fight it. So those two things push me towards getting it checked today, not reassuring you."

"You said you feel shivery and rough — have you been hot and cold, sweaty, any shaking chills? Have you taken your temperature? … Feeling like that, with the knee, tells me the infection might be affecting more than just the joint, which is another reason this can’t wait."

"Can I gently say something? You’ve said twice you don’t want to make a fuss or go in. After what happened to your wife in hospital, I completely understand why the thought of going is frightening — that fear makes total sense. But I’d be failing you if I let that stop me being honest: this is exactly the kind of thing where going in quickly is what protects you."

"Here’s the thing about an infected joint: left even a couple of days, it can damage the knee permanently, and the infection can spread. The hospital will take a sample of fluid from the joint with a needle — that’s how they tell infection from a flare — and treat it fast if needed. That’s why it’s today, not waiting to see."

"So I’m going to arrange for you to be seen at the hospital today — I’ll sort the referral so you’re expected. Is there someone who can take you, or shall I help with transport? Keep the leg rested. Keep eating and drinking as normal for now — with your diabetes, going without food at home is risky — and take your glucose meter and all your tablets with you; the hospital team will decide about the metformin and whether you need to fast for anything. If you become more unwell — high fever, shaking, confused — that’s a 999 call. I’ll check you got seen. You rang not wanting a fuss; going today is how I keep your knee, and you, safe."

f.learning: A single, acutely hot, swollen, red, painful joint with inability to weight-bear is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — a joint-destroying emergency that cannot be diagnosed or excluded by phone and must NOT be managed as "just an arthritis flare" with painkillers. The risk factors here stack damningly: a recent intra-articular steroid injection (a portal of entry that raises, not lowers, concern), diabetes (immunocompromise), age and pre-existing joint disease; and systemic upset (shivery, feverish) raises sepsis concern (screen by phone with the NICE NG253 red flags; his erratic glucose matters for his diabetes but is not itself an NG253 criterion) — though septic arthritis can be present without florid fever (BSR/BHPR 2006: treat as septic arthritis on high clinical suspicion even without fever). The action is urgent same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration (ideally before antibiotics), without advising nil by mouth at home in a man with diabetes, recognising that a crystal/OA history does not exclude infection (they coexist). The examinable hidden agenda is hospital fear driven by grief — his wife died after a hospital admission — making him minimise emergency features to stay home. Hear the fear and grief with compassion and use them to bring him to assessment, convey urgency without panic, refuse "wait it out", and confirm he goes.

knowledge.guideline: BSR/BHPR, BOA, RCGP and BSAC guideline for the management of the hot swollen joint in adults (2006; BSR update in development, scope 2025) · NICE NG253 (2025) — suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over · BNF (metformin, NSAIDs)
knowledge.summary: A single hot, red, swollen knee he cannot bear weight on, developing over 36 hours, 10 days after a steroid injection, in a man with diabetes who feels shivery, is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. He needs same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration before antibiotics — not stronger painkillers.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2006: a short history of a hot, swollen, tender joint with restricted movement should be regarded as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. It can destroy a joint quickly and carries a real mortality, especially in older people.

BSR/BHPR 2006: synovial fluid should be aspirated, Gram-stained and cultured before antibiotics are started, with crystal microscopy. That needs a hospital team the same day — it cannot be done or excluded by telephone.
Recent intra-articular injection, pre-existing joint disease, diabetes and older age all increase the risk. A recent steroid injection raises concern rather than explaining the swelling.
BSR/BHPR 2006: if clinical suspicion is high, treat as septic arthritis even without fever. Normal-looking systemic observations do not exclude it.

NICE NG253 (2025): assess anyone with suspected infection for sepsis. High-risk features include new confusion or altered mental state, respiratory rate 25 or more and heart rate over 130. By phone, ask about confusion, breathlessness, mottled or ashen skin and passing urine — any of these means a 999 ambulance.

points.h: Crystals and OA do not exclude infection
points.t: Gout, pseudogout and an OA flare can mimic sepsis and can coexist with it. Only aspiration separates them; a known arthritis history is not a diagnosis.

Infection pushes blood glucose up and dehydration adds risk with metformin (BNF: risk of lactic acidosis in conditions such as dehydration or severe infection). Ask him to bring his meter and medicines; the admitting team will decide on metformin.

dg.d: Identity checked; open question; told him he was right to call rather than letting “don’t want to fuss” shape the plan.
Recent bereavement, stoicism, fear of hospital, transport and who can take him.
Same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration (Gram stain, culture, crystals) before antibiotics, with bloods and blood glucose.
Septic arthritis, gout or pseudogout, OA flare, post-injection reaction; knows crystals and OA can coexist with infection.
Single joint, non-weight-bearing, systemic symptoms, NICE NG253 high-risk features asked (confusion, breathing, skin, urine).
States possible septic arthritis as the working diagnosis in plain language and explains why the injection and diabetes raise concern.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day hospital assessment, arranged by the GP; no antibiotics before aspiration; no painkiller-and-wait plan.
Diabetes: bring meter and medicines, keep hydrated; ibuprofen avoided; grief acknowledged with a plan to return to it.
999 sepsis triggers, fallback if no lift, GP checks he arrived, teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “Don’t want to make a fuss”, “shivery and rough” and the firm refusal of hospital each explored; the wife’s death surfaced gently.
Idea (an arthritis flare), hidden concern (hospital after his wife died there), expectation (stronger painkillers and rest at home).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of hospital after his wife died there following an admission ("people don’t come out"); he’s minimising emergency features to avoid going in, framing the recent injection as reassurance rather than a risk — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Whitcombe? It’s Dr Lee. Can I check your date of birth? … Thank you. What’s been happening with the knee?
model.why: Identity check and an open question

model.text: Sorry to bother you. It’s my arthritis knee — it’s blown up like a balloon over the last day or so, red hot, and I can’t put weight on it. Had a steroid jab in it last week. I just need stronger painkillers and I’ll rest it. Don’t want to make a fuss.

You’re not making a fuss at all — I’m glad you rang. I need to ask you some specific questions, because what you’re describing may need more than painkillers. Then we’ll decide together. Is that all right?
model.why: Validates the call and signals concern early without alarming

model.text: Go on.
Is it just the one knee? And is this different from your usual arthritis flare-ups?
model.why: Establishes a single joint and a change from baseline

model.text: Just the right one. It’s never been like this — can’t bend it at all, can’t stand on it.
How do you feel in yourself? Any shivers, sweats, feeling hot and cold? Have you checked your temperature?
Bit shivery, bit rough. I thought that was the pain. Haven’t got a thermometer.
Any confusion or muddled thinking, trouble breathing, going pale or blotchy, or passing much less urine?
model.why: Checks for NICE NG253 high-risk features that would need a 999 ambulance

model.text: No, nothing like that. Sugars have been all over the place, mind.
Thank you. Any cuts or skin infection near the knee, or any other joints swollen?
model.why: Other portals of entry and polyarticular disease

model.text: No, just that one.

Stan, I’m going to be honest because it matters. A single knee that’s suddenly hot, red, swollen and won’t take your weight — with you feeling shivery — isn’t a normal arthritis flare. It could be an infection inside the joint.
model.why: Names septic arthritis as the working concern

model.text: And the injection — I know it feels like the knee’s been seen to, but any injection into a joint can very occasionally let infection in. With diabetes too, your body finds infection harder to fight. Those make me more worried, not less.
model.why: Reframes the injection and diabetes as risk factors

model.text: An infected joint can be damaged within days, and the infection can spread into the blood. The only way to tell is for the hospital to draw some fluid off the knee with a needle — before any antibiotics — and treat it quickly if it’s infected. So this needs to be today.
model.why: Explains aspiration before antibiotics and why same-day

model.text: Hospital. No. I’d rather just sit it out here.
That sounded like a big ‘no’. Can I ask what going into hospital means for you right now?
model.why: Explores the resistance rather than overriding it

model.text: …My wife went in after a fall. She never came out. People don’t come out of there.
I’m so sorry, Stan. That’s a terrible loss, and so recent. Of course the thought of going in is frightening — anyone would feel that after what you’ve been through.
model.why: Acknowledges grief with compassion before persuading

model.text: I just keep thinking about her in that bed.

I understand. What I can tell you is that this is different: it’s one knee, you’re well enough to talk to me now, and going today is exactly what keeps it that way. The danger is in waiting. I wouldn’t be pushing if I didn’t think it mattered.
model.why: Uses his fear honestly to bring him to assessment, without false promises

model.text: …All right. If you really think so.
Thank you. I’ll phone the hospital team now so they’re expecting you and you won’t be sitting in a queue wondering. Is there someone who can take you? You mustn’t drive with that knee.
model.why: Direct referral, transport and driving safety

model.text: I’ll try to find someone. If not, I don’t know.

If nobody can take you within the hour, ring me back and I’ll arrange transport. Bring your tablets and your sugar meter. Don’t take any ibuprofen for now — paracetamol is fine for the pain until you’re seen. Keep sipping water.
model.why: Practical preparation; avoids NSAIDs; supports hydration with diabetes and metformin

model.text: If before you get there you become confused, very breathless, go blotchy or clammy, or feel much worse — call 999, don’t wait for a lift.
Can you tell me what you’re going to do after we hang up?
Find a lift, get to the hospital today with my tablets and meter. No ibuprofen. Ring you if I can’t get a lift, 999 if I get muddled or worse.

Exactly. I’ll ring the hospital this afternoon to check you’ve arrived. And when this is sorted, I’d like to talk with you about how you’re coping since your wife died — you shouldn’t be carrying that alone.
model.why: Commits to follow-up and returns to the grief

social.t: His wife’s death in hospital shapes how he sees admission. Acknowledge it, and plan a later conversation about grief, mood and support at home.
He cannot weight-bear or drive safely. Check who can take him and arrange hospital transport if no one can.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: adults are presumed to have capacity and may make unwise decisions. If he still refused, check he understands and can weigh the risks, document it, keep the door open, and safety-net clearly.
He should not drive while unable to bend or bear weight on the knee — he may not be able to control the vehicle safely.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): when remote assessment cannot meet a patient’s needs safely, arrange appropriate in-person care. Here that is same-day hospital assessment, not a GP visit next week.
Phoning the hospital team, confirming he arrived and documenting the advice given are part of safe care for an urgent referral.
If the injection was given in the practice, record the possible complication and consider a significant event review of the procedure — without assuming fault.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support and local bereavement services; Age UK for practical help at home during recovery.

redFlags: Single acutely hot, red, swollen knee over 36 hours; unable to weight-bear or bend it
Intra-articular steroid injection 10 days ago; type 2 diabetes; age 67
Shivery and unwell with erratic glucose — screen for sepsis (confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin, reduced urine)
psychosocial: Recently widowed; his wife died in hospital after a fall
Stoical: “don’t want to make a fuss”
Cannot drive or weight-bear — transport needed
ice: Idea: “It’s just my arthritis flaring after the injection”
Concern: hospital — “people don’t come out of there”
Expectation: stronger painkillers and resting it at home

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest: “A single knee that’s suddenly hot, swollen and won’t take your weight, with you feeling shivery after an injection, could be an infection in the joint. That can damage the knee within days, so it needs checking in hospital today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your knee is like a sealed room. If germs have got in, they can do a lot of damage quickly. The hospital needs to take a little fluid out with a needle to see what’s in there, and then treat it properly.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your wife, it makes complete sense that hospital feels like the last place you want to be. I’m asking you to go precisely so that this stays a knee problem and nothing more.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange transport, tell him the team will be expecting him, and promise a follow-up conversation about his grief.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration before antibiotics (BSR/BHPR 2006), arranged by the GP
No antibiotics or stronger painkillers as a substitute; avoid ibuprofen; paracetamol for pain meanwhile
Bring medicines and glucose meter; keep drinking fluids
safetyNet: Confusion, breathlessness, mottled or clammy skin, feeling much worse → 999 (new confusion is a NICE NG253 high-risk feature)
Ring back if no lift within the hour; GP checks he has arrived and follows up the grief afterwards

pitfalls.intro: This is an urgent-care station disguised as a painkiller request. It is failed by accepting the patient’s framing, by treating remotely, or by winning the argument about hospital without ever hearing why he is refusing.

items.fail: Prescribing stronger analgesia and advising rest for an “OA flare”.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” BSR/BHPR 2006: a hot, swollen, restricted joint is septic until proven otherwise.
items.fix: Name the concern out loud and arrange same-day hospital assessment.

items.fail: Seeing the recent steroid injection as the explanation.
items.why: Intra-articular injection is a recognised route for infection; it raises, not lowers, concern.
items.fix: “The injection makes me more worried, not less.”

items.fail: Starting oral antibiotics by phone to “cover it”.
items.why: Antibiotics before aspiration can prevent the organism being found and leave a joint half-treated.
items.fix: Explain that the hospital draws fluid off first, then treats.

items.fail: Not screening for sepsis because he “sounds all right”.
items.why: NICE NG253 asks for a sepsis assessment in suspected infection; high-risk features change the plan to 999.
items.fix: Ask about confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin and urine output, and give clear 999 triggers.

items.fail: Answering “I’d rather sit it out” with more facts and more pressure.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His refusal is about his wife’s death; arguing past it rarely works.
items.fix: “Can I ask what going into hospital means for you right now?” — then acknowledge before persuading.

items.fail: Telling him to go to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: A frightened, grieving man with no transport may simply not go; the plan must be workable.
items.fix: Phone the team, sort transport, give a fallback, and confirm he has arrived.

One joint or several, change from usual, weight-bearing, shivers, sweats, NG253 high-risk features, glucose, skin breaks. The injection 10 days ago.
Possible infected joint; the injection and diabetes raise the risk; aspiration before antibiotics, today.

GP phones the hospital team; transport; bring meter and tablets; no ibuprofen. 999 triggers. Teach-back; GP checks he arrived.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes stronger painkillers and advises rest; accepts “just arthritis”; treats the injection as reassuring; never asks about systemic symptoms; lets his refusal stand without exploring it; or starts antibiotics by phone.
wordPics.pass: Recognises possible septic arthritis; weights the injection and diabetes; asks about systemic upset; arranges same-day hospital assessment for aspiration; gives a sepsis safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores the refusal and hears his wife’s death with real compassion before persuading; is honest without false promises; arranges the referral and transport himself; practical diabetes advice; confirms he has arrived and plans to return to the grief.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like a flare after the injection — rest it and take some stronger painkillers.”
avoid.instead: “A single hot, swollen knee you can’t stand on isn’t a normal flare. It could be an infection, and that needs checking today.”
avoid.why: Treating a possible septic joint as a flare is the dangerous error the station tests.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send some antibiotics to the pharmacy to be on the safe side.”
avoid.instead: “The hospital needs to draw fluid off the knee first, so they can find the germ and give the right treatment.”
avoid.why: BSR/BHPR 2006: aspirate before antibiotics; blind antibiotics can mask the diagnosis.

avoid.dont: “You have to go in — there’s no choice.”
avoid.instead: “Can I ask what going into hospital means for you right now?”
avoid.why: Overriding him ignores his grief and makes refusal more likely; exploring it brings him with you.

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll try to find someone. If not, I don’t know.

If nobody can take you within the hour, ring me back and I’ll arrange transport. Bring your tablets and your sugar meter. Don’t take any ibuprofen for now — paracetamol is fine for the pain until you’re seen. Keep sipping water.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical preparation; avoids NSAIDs; supports hydration with diabetes and metformin

SCA_MODELS.text: If before you get there you become confused, very breathless, go blotchy or clammy, or feel much worse — call 999, don’t wait for a lift.
Can you tell me what you’re going to do after we hang up?
Find a lift, get to the hospital today with my tablets and meter. No ibuprofen. Ring you if I can’t get a lift, 999 if I get muddled or worse.

Exactly. I’ll ring the hospital this afternoon to check you’ve arrived. And when this is sorted, I’d like to talk with you about how you’re coping since your wife died — you shouldn’t be carrying that alone.
SCA_MODELS.why: Commits to follow-up and returns to the grief

SCA_STEM.name: Stan Whitcombe
SCA_STEM.recent: Intra-articular steroid injection, right knee, 10 days ago. Retired joiner. Recently bereaved (wife).
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request — “knee has blown up, wants stronger painkillers”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BSR/BHPR, BOA, RCGP and BSAC guideline for the management of the hot swollen joint in adults (2006; BSR update in development, scope 2025) · NICE NG253 (2025) — suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over · BNF (metformin, NSAIDs)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A single hot, red, swollen knee he cannot bear weight on, developing over 36 hours, 10 days after a steroid injection, in a man with diabetes who feels shivery, is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. He needs same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration before antibiotics — not stronger painkillers.

points.t: BSR/BHPR 2006: a short history of a hot, swollen, tender joint with restricted movement should be regarded as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. It can destroy a joint quickly and carries a real mortality, especially in older people.

BSR/BHPR 2006: synovial fluid should be aspirated, Gram-stained and cultured before antibiotics are started, with crystal microscopy. That needs a hospital team the same day — it cannot be done or excluded by telephone.
Recent intra-articular injection, pre-existing joint disease, diabetes and older age all increase the risk. A recent steroid injection raises concern rather than explaining the swelling.
BSR/BHPR 2006: if clinical suspicion is high, treat as septic arthritis even without fever. Normal-looking systemic observations do not exclude it.

NICE NG253 (2025): assess anyone with suspected infection for sepsis. High-risk features include new confusion or altered mental state, respiratory rate 25 or more and heart rate over 130. By phone, ask about confusion, breathlessness, mottled or ashen skin and passing urine — any of these means a 999 ambulance.

points.h: Crystals and OA do not exclude infection
points.t: Gout, pseudogout and an OA flare can mimic sepsis and can coexist with it. Only aspiration separates them; a known arthritis history is not a diagnosis.

Infection pushes blood glucose up and dehydration adds risk with metformin (BNF: risk of lactic acidosis in conditions such as dehydration or severe infection). Ask him to bring his meter and medicines; the admitting team will decide on metformin.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity checked; open question; told him he was right to call rather than letting “don’t want to fuss” shape the plan.
Recent bereavement, stoicism, fear of hospital, transport and who can take him.
“Don’t want to make a fuss”, “shivery and rough” and the firm refusal of hospital each explored; the wife’s death surfaced gently.
Idea (an arthritis flare), hidden concern (hospital after his wife died there), expectation (stronger painkillers and rest at home).
Same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration (Gram stain, culture, crystals) before antibiotics, with bloods and blood glucose.
Septic arthritis, gout or pseudogout, OA flare, post-injection reaction; knows crystals and OA can coexist with infection.
Single joint, non-weight-bearing, systemic symptoms, NICE NG253 high-risk features asked (confusion, breathing, skin, urine).
States possible septic arthritis as the working diagnosis in plain language and explains why the injection and diabetes raise concern.
Same-day hospital assessment, arranged by the GP; no antibiotics before aspiration; no painkiller-and-wait plan.
Diabetes: bring meter and medicines, keep hydrated; ibuprofen avoided; grief acknowledged with a plan to return to it.
999 sepsis triggers, fallback if no lift, GP checks he arrived, teach-back.

social.t: His wife’s death in hospital shapes how he sees admission. Acknowledge it, and plan a later conversation about grief, mood and support at home.
He cannot weight-bear or drive safely. Check who can take him and arrange hospital transport if no one can.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: adults are presumed to have capacity and may make unwise decisions. If he still refused, check he understands and can weigh the risks, document it, keep the door open, and safety-net clearly.
He should not drive while unable to bend or bear weight on the knee — he may not be able to control the vehicle safely.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): when remote assessment cannot meet a patient’s needs safely, arrange appropriate in-person care. Here that is same-day hospital assessment, not a GP visit next week.
Phoning the hospital team, confirming he arrived and documenting the advice given are part of safe care for an urgent referral.
If the injection was given in the practice, record the possible complication and consider a significant event review of the procedure — without assuming fault.

community.t: Cruse Bereavement Support and local bereavement services; Age UK for practical help at home during recovery.

redFlags: Single acutely hot, red, swollen knee over 36 hours; unable to weight-bear or bend it
Intra-articular steroid injection 10 days ago; type 2 diabetes; age 67
Shivery and unwell with erratic glucose — screen for sepsis (confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin, reduced urine)
psychosocial: Recently widowed; his wife died in hospital after a fall
Stoical: “don’t want to make a fuss”
Cannot drive or weight-bear — transport needed
ice: Idea: “It’s just my arthritis flaring after the injection”
Concern: hospital — “people don’t come out of there”
Expectation: stronger painkillers and resting it at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest: “A single knee that’s suddenly hot, swollen and won’t take your weight, with you feeling shivery after an injection, could be an infection in the joint. That can damage the knee within days, so it needs checking in hospital today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your knee is like a sealed room. If germs have got in, they can do a lot of damage quickly. The hospital needs to take a little fluid out with a needle to see what’s in there, and then treat it properly.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your wife, it makes complete sense that hospital feels like the last place you want to be. I’m asking you to go precisely so that this stays a knee problem and nothing more.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange transport, tell him the team will be expecting him, and promise a follow-up conversation about his grief.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for joint aspiration before antibiotics (BSR/BHPR 2006), arranged by the GP
No antibiotics or stronger painkillers as a substitute; avoid ibuprofen; paracetamol for pain meanwhile
Bring medicines and glucose meter; keep drinking fluids
safetyNet: Confusion, breathlessness, mottled or clammy skin, feeling much worse → 999 (new confusion is a NICE NG253 high-risk feature)
Ring back if no lift within the hour; GP checks he has arrived and follows up the grief afterwards

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is an urgent-care station disguised as a painkiller request. It is failed by accepting the patient’s framing, by treating remotely, or by winning the argument about hospital without ever hearing why he is refusing.

items.fail: Prescribing stronger analgesia and advising rest for an “OA flare”.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” BSR/BHPR 2006: a hot, swollen, restricted joint is septic until proven otherwise.
items.fix: Name the concern out loud and arrange same-day hospital assessment.

items.fail: Seeing the recent steroid injection as the explanation.
items.why: Intra-articular injection is a recognised route for infection; it raises, not lowers, concern.
items.fix: “The injection makes me more worried, not less.”

items.fail: Starting oral antibiotics by phone to “cover it”.
items.why: Antibiotics before aspiration can prevent the organism being found and leave a joint half-treated.
items.fix: Explain that the hospital draws fluid off first, then treats.

items.fail: Not screening for sepsis because he “sounds all right”.
items.why: NICE NG253 asks for a sepsis assessment in suspected infection; high-risk features change the plan to 999.
items.fix: Ask about confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin and urine output, and give clear 999 triggers.

items.fail: Answering “I’d rather sit it out” with more facts and more pressure.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His refusal is about his wife’s death; arguing past it rarely works.
items.fix: “Can I ask what going into hospital means for you right now?” — then acknowledge before persuading.

items.fail: Telling him to go to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: A frightened, grieving man with no transport may simply not go; the plan must be workable.
items.fix: Phone the team, sort transport, give a fallback, and confirm he has arrived.
